1324	get_previous_attempts(
1325	    feature="Image Classification"
1326	)
1327	```
1328	
1329	Response:
1330	
1331	```json
1332	{
1333	  "attempts": [
1334	    {
1335	      "version": "v8",
1336	      "change": "learning_rate=0.0001",
1337	      "status": "REGRESSION",
1338	      "result": "Accuracy dropped from 93.4% to 76.1%",
1339	      "recommendation": "Avoid repeating this configuration."
1340	    }
1341	  ]
1342	}
1343	```
1344	
1345	---
1346	
1347	# 38. MCP: get_version_diff
1348	
1349	Example:
1350	
1351	```text
1352	get_version_diff(
1353	    from_version="v6",
1354	    to_version="v7"
1355	)
1356	```
1357	
1358	Response should contain:
1359	
1360	```text
1361	changed files
1362	lines added
1363	lines removed
1364	exact diff
1365	metric changes
1366	test changes
1367	```
1368	
1369	---
1370	
1371	# 39. MCP: get_checkpoint_context
1372	
1373	Example:
1374	
1375	```text
1376	get_checkpoint_context(
1377	    version_id="v7"
1378	)
1379	```
1380	
1381	Response:
1382	
1383	```json
1384	{
1385	  "version": "v7",
1386	  "checkpoint_id": "checkpoint-abc123",
1387	  "agent": "Claude Code",
1388	  "intent": "Improve image classification accuracy",
1389	  "git_commit": "7fa91c"
1390	}
1391	```
1392	
1393	---
1394	
1395	# 40. MCP: get_development_trace
1396	
1397	This should provide the complete lineage.
1398	
1399	Example:
1400	
1401	```json
1402	{
1403	  "version": "v7",
1404	
1405	  "intent": "Improve image classification accuracy",
1406	
1407	  "agent": "Claude Code",
1408	
1409	  "entire": {
1410	    "checkpoint_id": "checkpoint-abc123"
1411	  },
1412	
1413	  "git": {
1414	    "commit": "7fa91c",
1415	    "parent": "91ac21"
1416	  },
1417	
1418	  "changes": {
1419	    "files": [
1420	      "model.py",
1421	      "preprocessing.py"
1422	    ],
1423	    "lines_added": 142,
1424	    "lines_removed": 37
1425	  },
1426	
1427	  "tests": {
1428	    "passed": 143,
1429	    "failed": 5
1430	  },
1431	
1432	  "metrics": {
1433	    "accuracy": {
1434	      "before": 89.2,
1435	      "after": 93.4
1436	    }
1437	  },
1438	
1439	  "status": "SUCCESS"
1440	}
1441	```
1442	
1443	---
1444	
1445	# 41. Databricks Normalized Event
1446	
1447	Every meaningful development version should be convertible into a Databricks event.
1448	
1449	Example:
1450	
1451	```json
1452	{
1453	  "project_id": "visionai",
1454	  "version_id": "v7",
1455	
1456	  "timestamp": "2026-09-06T01:20:00Z",
1457	
1458	  "source": "devmemory",
1459	
1460	  "checkpoint_id": "checkpoint-abc123",
1461	
1462	  "agent": "Claude Code",
1463	
1464	  "intent": "Improve image classification accuracy",
1465	
1466	  "feature": "Image Classification",
1467	
1468	  "git_commit": "7fa91c",
1469	
1470	  "parent_commit": "91ac21",
1471	
1472	  "status": "SUCCESS",
1473	
1474	  "files_changed": 2,
1475	
1476	  "lines_added": 142,
1477	  "lines_removed": 37,
1478	
1479	  "tests_passed": 143,
1480	  "tests_failed": 5,
1481	
1482	  "metrics": {
1483	    "accuracy_before": 89.2,
1484	    "accuracy_after": 93.4
1485	  },
1486	
1487	  "regression": false
1488	}
1489	```
1490	
1491	---
1492	
1493	# 42. Databricks Tables
1494	
1495	The initial Databricks model should contain:
1496	
1497	```text
1498	projects
1499	development_versions
1500	development_events
1501	features
1502	tests
1503	metrics
1504	agent_sessions
1505	```
1506	
1507	The implementation may simplify this for the MVP if necessary.
1508	
1509	The important requirement is that development data can be queried analytically.
1510	
1511	---
1512	
1513	# 43. Useful Databricks Queries
1514	
1515	The system should support analytics such as:
1516	
1517	### Regression history
1518	
1519	```text
1520	Which versions caused regressions?
1521	```
1522	
1523	### Feature attempts
1524	
1525	```text
1526	Which features required the most development attempts?
1527	```
1528	
1529	### Agent performance
1530	
1531	```text
1532	Which AI-assisted sessions produced the most successful changes?
1533	```
1534	
1535	### Frequently changed files
1536	
1537	```text
1538	Which files change most frequently?
1539	```
1540	
1541	### Development trend
1542	
1543	```text
1544	Are test results and metrics improving over time?
1545	```
1546	
1547	### Failed approaches
1548	
1549	```text
1550	Which approaches repeatedly failed?
1551	```
1552	
1553	These analytics should appear in the dashboard where practical.
1554	
1555	---
1556	
1557	# 44. Search
1558	
1559	Search should operate across normalized DevMemory metadata.
1560	
1561	Example:
1562	
1563	```http
1564	GET /api/search?q=authentication
1565	```
1566	
1567	Searchable fields should include:
1568	
1569	```text
1570	version ID
1571	intent
1572	agent
1573	feature
1574	status
1575	changed file paths
1576	commit SHA
1577	checkpoint ID
1578	analysis
1579	errors
1580	```
1581	
1582	Example results:
1583	
1584	```json
1585	{
1586	  "results": [
1587	    {
1588	      "version": "v3",
1589	      "type": "version",
1590	      "summary": "Added JWT authentication"
1591	    },
1592	    {
1593	      "version": "v7",
1594	      "type": "version",
1595	      "summary": "Modified authentication middleware"
1596	    }
1597	  ]
1598	}
1599	```
1600	
1601	---
1602	
1603	# 45. API Design Principle
1604	
1605	The API should expose development intelligence rather than database internals.
1606	
1607	Bad:
1608	
1609	```text
1610	GET /api/sql/versions
1611	```
1612	
1613	Good:
1614	
1615	```text
1616	GET /api/versions
1617	GET /api/context
1618	GET /api/attempts
1619	GET /api/features
1620	```
1621	
1622	The frontend and MCP layer should consume domain-level APIs.
1623	
1624	---
1625	
1626	# 46. Serialization
1627	
1628	Internal Python models should use typed structures.
1629	
1630	Prefer:
1631	
1632	```python
1633	@dataclass
1634	class DevelopmentVersion:
1635	    version_id: str
1636	    project_id: str
1637	    git_commit: str
1638	    parent_commit: str | None
1639	    intent: str | None
1640	    agent: str | None
1641	    status: str
1642	```
1643	
1644	Pydantic models can be used at API boundaries.
1645	
1646	Example:
1647	
1648	```python
1649	class VersionResponse(BaseModel):
1650	    version_id: str
1651	    git_commit: str
1652	    status: str
1653	```
1654	
1655	Keep persistence models and API response models separable where useful.
1656	
1657	---
1658	
1659	# 47. IDs
1660	
1661	Use stable identifiers.
1662	
1663	Recommended:
1664	
1665	```text
1666	project_id:
1667	human-readable slug
1668	
1669	version_id:
1670	v1, v2, v3...
1671	
1672	checkpoint_id:
1673	Entire-provided identifier
1674	
1675	git_commit:
1676	Git SHA
1677	
1678	artifact_id:
1679	UUID or deterministic artifact identifier
1680	```
1681	
1682	Version numbers are scoped to a project.
1683	
1684	---
1685	
1686	# 48. Version Creation Rules
1687	
1688	When:
1689	
1690	```bash
1691	devmemory checkpoint
1692	```
1693	
1694	is executed:
1695	
1696	```text
1697	1. Verify project is initialized.
1698	2. Verify Git repository exists.
1699	3. Inspect Git state.
1700	4. Discover relevant Entire checkpoint.
1701	5. Determine Git commit.
1702	6. Determine parent commit.
1703	7. Calculate changed files.
1704	8. Calculate diff statistics.
1705	9. Collect configured tests.
1706	10. Collect configured metrics.
1707	11. Determine feature.
1708	12. Determine status.
1709	13. Detect regression.
1710	14. Generate optional AI analysis.
1711	15. Create DevelopmentVersion.
1712	16. Store metadata in SQLite.
1713	17. Create artifact snapshot if enabled.
1714	18. Send normalized event to Databricks.
1715	19. Update dashboard data.
1716	```
1717	
1718	The entire operation should be traceable.
1719	
1720	---
1721	
1722	# 49. Idempotency
1723	
1724	Running:
1725	
1726	```bash
1727	devmemory checkpoint
1728	```
1729	
1730	twice for the same Git commit should not create duplicate versions accidentally.
1731	
1732	Before creating a new version:
1733	
1734	```text
1735	Check whether git_commit already belongs to a DevMemory version.
1736	```
1737	
1738	If it does:
1739	
1740	```text
1741	Version already exists for commit 7fa91c.
1742	
1743	Version: V7
1744	```
1745	
1746	Allow an explicit force option only if needed.
1747	
1748	---
1749	
1750	# 50. MVP Simplifications
1751	
1752	The following may be simplified during initial implementation:
1753	
1754	```text
1755	Advanced semantic search
1756	Complex feature detection
1757	Automatic metric discovery
1758	Automatic documentation analysis
1759	Sophisticated graph analysis
1760	Multiple artifact backends
1761	Complex Databricks architecture
1762	Advanced MCP authentication
1763	Distributed storage
1764	```
1765	
1766	The core data model must remain capable of supporting these later.
1767	
1768	---
1769	
1770	# 51. MVP Definition of Done
1771	
1772	The data/API layer is complete when the following flow works:
1773	
1774	```text
1775	Entire Checkpoint
1776	        ↓
1777	Git Commit
1778	        ↓
1779	DevelopmentEvent
1780	        ↓
1781	DevelopmentVersion
1782	        ↓
1783	SQLite
1784	        ↓
1785	REST API
1786	        ↓
1787	Dashboard
1788	```
1789	
1790	And the same version can provide context to an AI agent:
1791	
1792	```text
1793	DevelopmentVersion
1794	        ↓
1795	Project Context
1796	        ↓
1797	MCP/API
1798	        ↓
1799	Future AI Agent
1800	```
1801	
1802	The minimum useful version record must answer:
1803	
1804	```text
1805	What changed?
1806	Why did it change?
1807	Which AI agent worked on it?
1808	Which Entire checkpoint is associated?
1809	Which Git commit contains the change?
1810	Which files changed?
1811	What was the result?
1812	Did tests pass?
1813	Did metrics improve?
1814	Was this a regression?
1815	What should happen next?
1816	```
1817	
1818	This data model is the foundation of DevMemory.
1819

# DevMemory — Data & API Specification

## 1. Purpose

This document defines the data structures, local database model, external analytics schema, REST API, and AI/MCP interface for DevMemory.

The goal is to create one normalized representation of a development change that connects:

```text
Intent
   ↓
AI Agent
   ↓
Entire Checkpoint
   ↓
Git Commit
   ↓
Git Diff
   ↓
Tests
   ↓
Metrics
   ↓
Development Version
   ↓
Analysis
   ↓
Project Memory
````

DevMemory should use existing systems as sources of truth rather than duplicating their responsibilities.

---

# 2. Source-of-Truth Model

| Information              | Source of Truth           |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| Source code              | Git                       |
| Git history              | Git                       |
| Git diff                 | Git                       |
| AI development context   | Entire                    |
| Entire Checkpoint        | Entire                    |
| Local DevMemory metadata | SQLite                    |
| Development versions     | DevMemory                 |
| Feature history          | DevMemory                 |
| Test results             | DevMemory                 |
| Development metrics      | DevMemory                 |
| Project memory           | DevMemory                 |
| Analytics                | Databricks                |
| Artifacts/snapshots      | Filesystem/object storage |
| AI context interface     | DevMemory API/MCP         |

DevMemory should store references to external sources wherever possible.

---

# 3. Core Entity Relationship

The main relationship is:

```text
Project
   │
   ├── Features
   │
   └── Development Versions
           │
           ├── Entire Checkpoints
           │
           ├── Git Commit
           │
           ├── Changed Files
           │
           ├── Tests
           │
           ├── Metrics
           │
           ├── Artifacts
           │
           └── Analysis
```

A development version represents a meaningful development event.

It is not simply a Git commit.

---

# 4. Project

A project represents one repository being tracked by DevMemory.

Example:

```json
{
  "project_id": "visionai",
  "name": "VisionAI",
  "repository_path": "/projects/visionai",
  "created_at": "2026-09-06T01:00:00Z",
  "current_version_id": "v7"
}
```

Fields:

```text
project_id
name
repository_path
created_at
updated_at
current_version_id
```

---

# 5. DevelopmentVersion

This is the central entity.

Example:

```json
{
  "version_id": "v7",
  "project_id": "visionai",

  "intent": "Improve image classification accuracy",

  "agent": "Claude Code",

  "entire_checkpoint_id": "checkpoint-abc123",

  "git_commit": "7fa91c",
  "parent_commit": "91ac21",

  "feature_id": "image-classification",

  "status": "SUCCESS",

  "tests_passed": 143,
  "tests_failed": 5,

  "metrics": {
    "accuracy": {
      "before": 89.2,
      "after": 93.4
    }
  },

  "lines_added": 142,
  "lines_removed": 37,

  "created_at": "2026-09-06T01:20:00Z"
}
```

Required fields:

```text
version_id
project_id
git_commit
created_at
status
```

Recommended fields:

```text
intent
agent
parent_commit
entire_checkpoint_id
feature_id
tests
metrics
analysis
artifact
```

---

# 6. Version Status

Supported statuses:

```text
SUCCESS
PARTIAL_SUCCESS
ERROR
REGRESSION
IN_PROGRESS
NEEDS_REVIEW
```

Status should represent the development result rather than merely whether the Git commit exists.

Example:

```text
Git commit exists
+
Tests fail
+
Performance worsened
=
REGRESSION
```

---

# 7. EntireCheckpoint

DevMemory should store a lightweight representation of an Entire checkpoint.

Example:

```json
{
  "checkpoint_id": "checkpoint-abc123",
  "location": "entire://checkpoint/abc123",
  "agent": "Claude Code",
  "intent": "Improve image classification accuracy",
  "timestamp": "2026-09-06T01:15:00Z",
  "git_commit": "7fa91c",
  "association_method": "explicit",
  "association_confidence": 1.0
}
```

Fields:

```text
checkpoint_id
location
agent
intent
timestamp
git_commit
association_method
association_confidence
metadata
```

Do not duplicate the complete Entire checkpoint.

---

# 8. GitReference

Git data should be represented as references.

Example:

```json
{
  "commit": "7fa91c",
  "parent_commit": "91ac21",
  "branch": "main"
}
```

Git should be queried whenever the exact diff or history is required.

DevMemory does not become a second Git implementation.

---

# 9. ChangedFile

A version can contain multiple changed files.

Example:

```json
{
  "path": "model.py",
  "change_type": "modified",
  "lines_added": 80,
  "lines_removed": 22
}
```

Supported change types:

```text
added
modified
deleted
renamed
```

Fields:

```text
version_id
path
change_type
old_path
lines_added
lines_removed
```

---

# 10. Git Diff

The exact Git diff should be generated from Git.

Example:

```diff
- learning_rate = 0.001
+ learning_rate = 0.0001

+ scheduler = ReduceLROnPlateau(...)
```

The MVP may store the diff for convenient display.

However, Git remains the source of truth.

The system should also be able to reconstruct:

```bash
git diff <parent_commit> <commit>
```

---

# 11. Feature

Features represent logical parts of the project.

Example:

```json
{
  "feature_id": "image-classification",
  "project_id": "visionai",
  "name": "Image Classification",
  "status": "COMPLETE"
}
```

Supported feature statuses:

```text
COMPLETE
PARTIAL
IN_PROGRESS
FAILED
NOT_STARTED
```

A feature can have many development versions.

Example:

```text
Image Classification

V3 → SUCCESS
V4 → SUCCESS
V5 → REGRESSION
V6 → SUCCESS
V7 → SUCCESS
```

---

# 12. TestResult

Tests are associated with a development version.

Example:

```json
{
  "version_id": "v7",
  "total": 148,
  "passed": 143,
  "failed": 5,
  "skipped": 0,
  "duration_seconds": 42.7,
  "command": "pytest"
}
```

Fields:

```text
version_id
total
passed
failed
skipped
duration_seconds
command
output
```

The MVP should support command-based test collection.

Example:

```bash
pytest
```

The system should capture:

```text
exit code
stdout
stderr
duration
pass/fail counts
```

Do not attempt to support every testing framework automatically in the MVP.

---

# 13. Metric

Metrics are arbitrary project measurements.

DevMemory must not assume that every project is an ML project.

Example ML metric:

```json
{
  "name": "accuracy",
  "before": 89.2,
  "after": 93.4,
  "unit": "%"
}
```

Example software metric:

```json
{
  "name": "latency",
  "before": 420,
  "after": 310,
  "unit": "ms"
}
```

Example:

```json
{
  "name": "error_rate",
  "before": 4.2,
  "after": 1.7,
  "unit": "%"
}
```

Schema:

```text
metric_id
version_id
name
before_value
after_value
unit
direction
metadata
```

`direction` may be:

```text
higher_is_better
lower_is_better
neutral
```

---

# 14. Regression

A regression represents a measurable deterioration caused by a development version.

Example:

```json
{
  "version_id": "v8",
  "metric": "accuracy",
  "before": 93.4,
  "after": 76.1,
  "change_percent": -18.5,
  "severity": "HIGH"
}
```

Regression detection can initially use simple rules.

Example:

```text
If metric direction = higher_is_better
and after < before
then possible regression.
```

For:

```text
lower_is_better
```

the opposite applies.

Test regressions can include:

```text
previously passing tests → failing tests
```

---

# 15. DevelopmentEvent

A normalized event allows different adapters to feed the same system.

Example:

```json
{
  "event_id": "event-123",
  "project_id": "visionai",

  "timestamp": "2026-09-06T01:20:00Z",

  "source": "devmemory",

  "checkpoint_id": "checkpoint-abc123",

  "agent": "Claude Code",

  "intent": "Improve image classification accuracy",

  "git_commit": "7fa91c",
  "parent_commit": "91ac21",

  "changed_files": [
    "model.py",
    "preprocessing.py"
  ],

  "feature": "Image Classification",

  "status": "SUCCESS",

  "tests": {
    "passed": 143,
    "failed": 5
  },

  "metrics": {
    "accuracy": {
      "before": 89.2,
      "after": 93.4
    }
  }
}
```

The normalized event is the bridge between adapters and storage.

---

# 16. Analysis

AI-generated analysis should be stored separately from raw development information.

Example:

```json
{
  "summary": "Preprocessing changes improved classification accuracy.",
  "reasoning": "Normalization reduced input variance.",
  "recommendation": "Keep this approach.",
  "warnings": []
}
```

Important:

AI analysis must never overwrite factual source information.

For example:

```text
Git says:
142 lines added
```

AI analysis cannot change that to:

```text
approximately 150 lines
```

The system should distinguish:

```text
FACT
```

from:

```text
AI ANALYSIS
```

---

# 17. PreviousAttempt

Previous attempts are derived from historical development versions.

Example:

```json
{
  "version_id": "v8",
  "feature": "Image Classification",
  "change_summary": "Changed learning rate to 0.0001",
  "status": "REGRESSION",
  "result": "Accuracy dropped from 93.4% to 76.1%"
}
```

The MVP can retrieve previous attempts using:

1. Same feature.
2. Same files.
3. Similar intent.
4. Similar metric.
5. Explicitly failed/regressed versions.

Semantic similarity can be added later.

---

# 18. Artifact

An artifact represents a snapshot associated with a version.

Example:

```json
{
  "artifact_id": "artifact-v7",
  "version_id": "v7",
  "path": ".devmemory/artifacts/v7.tar.gz",
  "type": "project_snapshot",
  "size_bytes": 382910,
  "created_at": "2026-09-06T01:21:00Z"
}
```

The MVP should use compressed project archives.

Do not build container-based reproducibility.

---

# 19. Environment Metadata

Optionally store:

```json
{
  "python_version": "3.12.5",
  "platform": "Windows",
  "package_manager": "pip"
}
```

Potential additional metadata:

```text
requirements.txt
pyproject.toml
package.json
lock files
OS
runtime version
```

This is metadata only.

Do not attempt to recreate the entire environment.

---

# 20. SQLite Database

The MVP should use SQLite.

Recommended database:

```text
.devmemory/metadata.db
```

---

# 21. Projects Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE projects (
    project_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    repository_path TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    current_version_id TEXT
);
```

---

# 22. Versions Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE versions (
    version_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    project_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    intent TEXT,
    agent TEXT,

    entire_checkpoint_id TEXT,

    git_commit TEXT NOT NULL,
    parent_commit TEXT,

    feature_id TEXT,

    status TEXT NOT NULL,

    lines_added INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    lines_removed INTEGER DEFAULT 0,

    analysis_json TEXT,

    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY(project_id)
        REFERENCES projects(project_id),

    FOREIGN KEY(feature_id)
        REFERENCES features(feature_id)
);
```

---

# 23. Features Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE features (
    feature_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    project_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,

    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    updated_at TEXT NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY(project_id)
        REFERENCES projects(project_id)
);
```

---

# 24. Changed Files Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE changed_files (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,

    version_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    path TEXT NOT NULL,
    old_path TEXT,

    change_type TEXT NOT NULL,

    lines_added INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    lines_removed INTEGER DEFAULT 0,

    FOREIGN KEY(version_id)
        REFERENCES versions(version_id)
);
```

---

# 25. Tests Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE tests (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,

    version_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    command TEXT,

    total INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    passed INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    failed INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    skipped INTEGER DEFAULT 0,

    duration_seconds REAL,

    output TEXT,

    FOREIGN KEY(version_id)
        REFERENCES versions(version_id)
);
```

---

# 26. Metrics Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE metrics (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,

    version_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    name TEXT NOT NULL,

    before_value REAL,
    after_value REAL,

    unit TEXT,

    direction TEXT,

    metadata_json TEXT,

    FOREIGN KEY(version_id)
        REFERENCES versions(version_id)
);
```

---

# 27. Artifacts Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE artifacts (
    artifact_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,

    version_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    path TEXT NOT NULL,

    type TEXT NOT NULL,

    size_bytes INTEGER,

    created_at TEXT NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY(version_id)
        REFERENCES versions(version_id)
);
```

---

# 28. Entire Checkpoints Table

```sql
CREATE TABLE entire_checkpoints (
    checkpoint_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,

    project_id TEXT NOT NULL,

    location TEXT,

    agent TEXT,

    intent TEXT,

    timestamp TEXT,

    git_commit TEXT,

    association_method TEXT,

    association_confidence REAL,

    metadata_json TEXT,

    FOREIGN KEY(project_id)
        REFERENCES projects(project_id)
);
```

---

# 29. Database Indexes

Add indexes for common queries:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_versions_project
ON versions(project_id);

CREATE INDEX idx_versions_git_commit
ON versions(git_commit);

CREATE INDEX idx_versions_feature
ON versions(feature_id);

CREATE INDEX idx_versions_status
ON versions(status);

CREATE INDEX idx_changed_files_path
ON changed_files(path);

CREATE INDEX idx_metrics_name
ON metrics(name);

CREATE INDEX idx_checkpoints_commit
ON entire_checkpoints(git_commit);
```

---

# 30. Version Comparison

The comparison API should accept:

```text
version_a
version_b
```

Example:

```text
V6 → V7
```

The backend should:

1. Resolve V6 to its Git commit.
2. Resolve V7 to its Git commit.
3. Generate the Git diff.
4. Compare changed files.
5. Compare tests.
6. Compare metrics.
7. Compare status.
8. Compare feature state.

Example response:

```json
{
  "from_version": "v6",
  "to_version": "v7",

  "git": {
    "from_commit": "91ac21",
    "to_commit": "7fa91c",
    "lines_added": 142,
    "lines_removed": 37
  },

  "files": [
    "model.py",
    "preprocessing.py"
  ],

  "metrics": {
    "accuracy": {
      "before": 89.2,
      "after": 93.4
    }
  },

  "tests": {
    "before_passed": 138,
    "after_passed": 143
  },

  "status": "SUCCESS"
}
```

---

# 31. Restore

Restore should operate using Git.

The API:

```text
POST /api/versions/{version_id}/restore
```

should NOT immediately destroy the current state.

Preferred MVP behavior:

```text
1. Check working tree.
2. Refuse if there are uncommitted changes unless explicitly overridden.
3. Identify target Git commit.
4. Create a safety reference/current-state record.
5. Restore the requested state.
6. Inform the user.
```

The UI must clearly warn:

```text
Restore Version 10

This will restore the project source code to the Git state
associated with Version 10.

Current uncommitted changes may be affected.
```

---

# 32. REST API

The backend should expose a simple REST API.

Base:

```text
/api
```

---

## Project

```http
GET /api/project
```

Returns project information.

---

## Status

```http
GET /api/status
```

Example:

```json
{
  "current_version": "v14",
  "completion": 82,
  "features": {
    "completed": 8,
    "total": 10
  },
  "tests": {
    "passed": 143,
    "failed": 5
  }
}
```

---

## Versions

```http
GET /api/versions
```

Returns version history.

Optional:

```http
GET /api/versions/{version_id}
```

Returns complete version information.

---

## Version Diff

```http
GET /api/versions/{version_id}/diff
```

Returns the exact Git diff associated with the version.

---

## Compare

```http
GET /api/compare?from=v6&to=v7
```

Returns comparison data.

---

## Features

```http
GET /api/features
```

Returns feature status.

```http
GET /api/features/{feature_id}
```

Returns feature history.

---

## Previous Attempts

```http
GET /api/attempts
```

Returns previous development attempts.

Optional filters:

```text
feature
status
query
```

---

## Checkpoint

```http
GET /api/versions/{version_id}/checkpoint
```

Returns Entire checkpoint information.

---

## Context

```http
GET /api/context
```

Returns AI-oriented project context.

---

## Restore

```http
POST /api/versions/{version_id}/restore
```

Restores a previous version after safety checks.

The important requirement is that development data can be queried analytically.

# 43. Useful Databricks Queries

The system should support analytics such as:

### Regression history

```text
Which versions caused regressions?
```

### Feature attempts

```text
Which features required the most development attempts?
```

### Agent performance

```text
Which AI-assisted sessions produced the most successful changes?
```

### Frequently changed files

```text
Which files change most frequently?
```

### Development trend

```text
Are test results and metrics improving over time?
```

### Failed approaches

```text
Which approaches repeatedly failed?
```

These analytics should appear in the dashboard where practical.

Search should operate across normalized DevMemory metadata.

Example:


Searchable fields should include:

```text
analysis
```

```json
      "type": "version",

    },

      "type": "version",
      "summary": "Modified authentication middleware"
    }
  ]
```

# 45. API Design Principle

The API should expose development intelligence rather than database internals.

Bad:

```text
GET /api/sql/versions
```

Good:

```text
GET /api/versions
GET /api/context
GET /api/attempts
GET /api/features
```

The frontend and MCP layer should consume domain-level APIs.

---

# 46. Serialization

Internal Python models should use typed structures.

Prefer:

```python
@dataclass
class DevelopmentVersion:
    version_id: str
    project_id: str
    git_commit: str
    parent_commit: str | None
    intent: str | None
    agent: str | None
    status: str
```

Pydantic models can be used at API boundaries.

Example:

```python
class VersionResponse(BaseModel):
    version_id: str
    git_commit: str
    status: str
```

Keep persistence models and API response models separable where useful.

---

# 47. IDs

Use stable identifiers.

Recommended:

```text
project_id:
human-readable slug

version_id:
v1, v2, v3...

checkpoint_id:
Entire-provided identifier

git_commit:
Git SHA

artifact_id:
UUID or deterministic artifact identifier
```

Version numbers are scoped to a project.

---

# 48. Version Creation Rules

When:

```bash
devmemory checkpoint
```

is executed:

```text
1. Verify project is initialized.
2. Verify Git repository exists.
3. Inspect Git state.
4. Discover relevant Entire checkpoint.
5. Determine Git commit.
6. Determine parent commit.
7. Calculate changed files.
8. Calculate diff statistics.
9. Collect configured tests.
10. Collect configured metrics.
11. Determine feature.
12. Determine status.
13. Detect regression.
14. Generate optional AI analysis.
15. Create DevelopmentVersion.
16. Store metadata in SQLite.
17. Create artifact snapshot if enabled.
18. Send normalized event to Databricks.
19. Update dashboard data.
```

The entire operation should be traceable.

---

# 49. Idempotency

Running:

```bash
devmemory checkpoint
```

twice for the same Git commit should not create duplicate versions accidentally.

Before creating a new version:

```text
Check whether git_commit already belongs to a DevMemory version.
```

If it does:

```text
Version already exists for commit 7fa91c.

Version: V7
```

Allow an explicit force option only if needed.

---

# 50. MVP Simplifications

The following may be simplified during initial implementation:

```text
Advanced semantic search
Complex feature detection
Automatic metric discovery
Automatic documentation analysis
Sophisticated graph analysis
Multiple artifact backends
Complex Databricks architecture
Advanced MCP authentication
Distributed storage
```

The core data model must remain capable of supporting these later.

---

# 51. MVP Definition of Done

The data/API layer is complete when the following flow works:

```text
Entire Checkpoint
        ↓
Git Commit
        ↓
DevelopmentEvent
        ↓
DevelopmentVersion
        ↓
SQLite
        ↓
REST API
        ↓
Dashboard
```

And the same version can provide context to an AI agent:

```text
DevelopmentVersion
        ↓
Project Context
        ↓
MCP/API
        ↓
Future AI Agent
```

The minimum useful version record must answer:

```text
What changed?
Why did it change?
Which AI agent worked on it?
Which Entire checkpoint is associated?
Which Git commit contains the change?
Which files changed?
What was the result?
Did tests pass?
Did metrics improve?
Was this a regression?
What should happen next?
```

This data model is the foundation of DevMemory.

## Entire Checkpoint Overview

Entire CLI hooks into your Git workflow to capture AI agent sessions as you work, and sessions are indexed alongside commits, creating a searchable record of how code was written in your repo.

## How Checkpoints Work

When you commit, work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an Entire-Checkpoint trailer. A 12-character hex checkpoint ID is added as a trailer in commit messages, creating a bidirectional link between the code change and its reasoning context.

## Key Features

Entire creates a checkpoint for every commit: the code change paired with the agent session that produced it, and stores all your code, together with every session, prompt, and tool call. It stores agent transcripts, prompts, and tool calls on a separate branch so every commit answers both what changed and why.

## Git Integration

All session data lives on a dedicated branch called entire/checkpoints/v1, keeping the main branch clean for standard code review workflows. The CLI detects which AI coding agent is active and configures accordingly, supporting Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, and GitHub Copilot CLI.

## Hackathon Use

The Sentiment-Maxxers used Entire to preserve agent context, audit AI-generated code, and win the hackathon challenge at the Big Berlin Hack.

# Entire CLI: Comprehensive Reference

## Core Concept

Entire captures AI agent sessions alongside Git commits, creating a searchable record of how code was written. Sessions are stored separately from branch history in checkpoint refs.

## Installation

**macOS/Linux:**
```
brew tap entireio/tap && brew install --cask entire
# or: curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
```

**Windows:**
```
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Go:**
```
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest
```

## Setup Commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `entire enable` | Initialize Entire in repository |
| `entire disable` | Remove git hooks |
| `entire status` | Check current status (`--json` available) |
| `entire agent add/remove/list` | Manage agent integrations |
| `entire configure` | Update non-agent settings |
| `entire doctor` | Diagnose and fix issues |

## Session & Checkpoint Commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `entire session list/info/current/stop` | Manage sessions |
| `entire session resume <branch>` | Restore previous session metadata |
| `entire checkpoint list/explain/search` | Query checkpoint data |
| `entire search` | Semantic and keyword matching |
| `entire activity` | Activity overview |
| `entire recap` | Summarize recent checkpoints |

## Checkpoint Architecture

**Storage Location:** `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`

**Checkpoint ID Format:** 26-character ULIDs (e.g., `REDACTED`), sortable by creation time. Legacy 12-character hex IDs also supported.

**Git Trailer:** Commits include `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` linking work to checkpoints.

**Contents:** Each checkpoint ref points to a commit containing `metadata.json`, per-session transcripts, and subagent task records.

## Configuration Files

**`.entire/settings.json` (committed):**
```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "checkpoints": {
    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
  },
  "telemetry": true,
  "commit_linking": "prompt",
  "strategy_options": {
    "push_sessions": true,
    "checkpoint_remote": {
      "provider": "github",
      "repo": "org/repo"
    }
  },
  "summary_generation": {
    "provider": "claude-code",
    "model": "sonnet"
  }
}
```

**`.entire/settings.local.json` (gitignored):**
Personal overrides with same schema.

**Agent Hooks Locations:**
- Claude Code: `.claude/settings.json`
- Cursor: `.cursor/hooks.json`
- Codex: `.codex/hooks.json`
- Gemini: `.gemini/settings.json`
- Copilot CLI: `.github/hooks/entire.json`
- OpenCode: `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts`
- Pi: `.pi/extensions/entire/index.ts`

## Agent Detection

Entire automatically detects active agents by checking for installed hooks in their respective directories—no registry needed.

**Supported Agents:** Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Factory AI Droid.

## Enable Flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--agent <name>` | Specify agent (non-interactive) |
| `--yes, -y` | Accept defaults |
| `--force, -f` | Reinstall hooks |
| `--checkpoint-remote` | Separate checkpoint repository |
| `--skip-push-sessions` | Disable auto-push |
| `--local` | Write to `.settings.local.json` |
| `--import-history` | Import existing sessions |
| `--search-skill` | Install search extension |
| `--telemetry=false` | Disable analytics |

## Authentication

**Standard:** `entire login` opens browser, stores tokens in OS keyring.

**Headless:**
```bash
ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
# Tokens written to `~/.config/entire/tokens.json` (mode 0600)
```

**CI/Automation:**
```bash
ENTIRE_TOKEN=<JWT> entire status
# No disk I/O; token derived from control plane endpoint
```

## Security & Privacy

Session transcripts stored in checkpoint refs. **Public repos expose this data.** Entire redacts detected secrets (API keys, tokens) before writing checkpoints—best-effort only. Temporary shadow branches hold unredacted code snapshots; never push manually. Shadow branches never pushed automatically.

Configurable redaction layers available in `.entire/settings.json` under `redaction.*`.

## Output Options

Commands supporting structured output:
- `entire status --json` → JSON
- `entire checkpoint list --json` → JSON
- `entire session list --json` → JSON

## Checkpoint Explanation

`entire checkpoint explain <id>` displays checkpoint metadata. With `--generate`, uses configured agent to create AI summary:

```bash
entire configure --summarize-provider codex
entire checkpoint explain <id> --generate
```

Default summarizer: Claude Code (model: sonnet).

## Checkpoint Remote Configuration

**Single-remote election (default):**
Checkpoints pushed to first elected remote (captured from habits, then `origin`, then sole remote).

**Dedicated checkpoint repo:**
```bash
entire enable --checkpoint-remote github:org/checkpoints-private
```

**Token override:**
```bash
ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN=<token> git push
```

Entire converts inherited checkpoint_remote in upstream repos to fallback-only, preventing accidental upstream pollution.

## Configuration Priority

Local settings override project settings field-by-field, except:
- `checkpoints` block replaced wholesale
- Tracked `.settings.local.json` ignored entirely

## Debug & Cleanup

```bash
ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug entire status
entire doctor                    # Diagnose
entire doctor bundle            # Redacted diagnostic
entire clean --force            # Current commit
entire clean --all --force      # Repo-wide
```

## Workflow Example

1. `entire enable --agent claude-code`
2. Work with agent
3. `entire status` (check session)
4. Commit code
5. `entire session resume <branch>` (restore context)

## Plugins

External commands (kubectl-style): `entire-<name>` on `$PATH` → `entire <name>`

```bash
entire plugin search
entire plugin install run
entire plugin list
entire plugin remove run
```

Remote installs: newest stable semver tag auto-resolved, asset verified against `checksums.txt`.

## Notable Omissions

No mention of "Entire Graph" or MCP integration in provided content. Tool calling and token usage tracked but not detailed. Subagent capture limited (Pi excluded).

# Complete Reference: `entire checkpoint`

## Command Overview
The tool provides four primary subcommands for managing checkpoints: list, explain, tokens, and search.

## Subcommand: `checkpoint list`
**Purpose:** "List checkpoints on the current branch."

**Key Flags:**
- `--json`: JSON output format
- `--no-pager`: Disable pagination
- `--pending`: Shows live session rewind points instead of condensed checkpoints
- `--session ID`: Filter by session identifier

## Subcommand: `checkpoint explain`
**Purpose:** "Generate an AI-powered explanation of a session or commit."

**Key Flags:**
- `-c, --checkpoint ID`: Target specific checkpoint
- `--commit SHA`: Target specific commit using SHA or reference
- `--generate`: "Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint"
- `--full`: Display complete transcript with all interactions
- `--short`: "Show summary only (omit prompts and files)"
- `--raw-transcript`: Display raw JSONL transcript file
- `--search-all`: Search without branch/depth restrictions

**Getting checkpoint for a commit:** Use `--commit SHA` parameter or search for commits carrying an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.

**Documented return fields:** The documentation lists these potential elements—prompts, files, and session data—but doesn't specify exact field names or complete output schema.

## Subcommand: `checkpoint tokens`
**Purpose:** Display "token usage and optimization recommendations."

**Key Flags:**
- `--json`: JSON output
- `--agent-brief`: Compact guidance for agents
- `--compare ID`: Baseline comparison functionality

## Subcommand: `checkpoint search`
**Purpose:** "Search checkpoints using semantic and keyword matching."

**Key Flags:**
- `--code`: Search code content rather than checkpoint metadata
- `--author NAME`, `--branch NAME`: Filter parameters
- `--date PERIOD`: Temporal filtering (week/month)
- `--json`, `--compact`: Output formats
- `--limit N`, `--page N`: Pagination controls

# Checkpoint Inspection Guide

## Core Commands

The Entire CLI provides several ways to work with checkpoints from your terminal:

**List checkpoints:** `entire checkpoint list` displays all checkpoints on the current branch. Adding `--json` provides machine-readable output, while `--session ID` filters to a specific session.

**Search checkpoints:** When you're unsure which checkpoint to examine, use `entire checkpoint search "what changed"` to locate them by phrase, meaning, or context.

**Explain checkpoints:** Run `entire checkpoint explain CHECKPOINT_ID` to get details about a specific checkpoint. You can use an abbreviated ID prefix or reference a commit with `entire checkpoint explain HEAD~3`.

## Output Options

The explain command supports several flags:
- `--full`: Returns the complete parsed transcript
- `--raw-transcript`: Provides the raw JSONL file
- `--short`: Shows only the summary
- `--generate`: Creates an AI-generated summary (requires configured provider CLI)

## Token Analysis

The `entire checkpoint tokens CHECKPOINT_ID` command "report[s] token usage and optimization recommendations" including model information, branch details, and usage breakdowns.

Compare two checkpoints with: `entire checkpoint tokens CHECKPOINT_ID --compare BASELINE_ID` to see how token consumption shifted between them.

Additional flags: `--json` (JSON output), `--agent-brief` (compact guidance).

## Available Metadata

The documentation doesn't explicitly list specific metadata fields, but commands reference: checkpoint names, sessions, agents, models used, branches, and token metrics.

# Overview of `entire why`

The `entire why` command helps you trace the origin of code by revealing the commit, checkpoint, prompt, and session associated with a specific file or line.

## Basic Usage

The command follows this syntax:
```bash
entire why FILE[:LINE] [flags]
```

## Key Capabilities

You can investigate context at different levels:
- **File level**: `entire why overview.mdx`
- **Specific line**: `entire why overview.mdx:12` or using `--line 12`
- **JSON output**: Add the `--json` flag for structured results

## Available Flags

Two main options modify the command's behavior:
- `--line LINE`: Targets a specific line number
- `--json`: Returns results in JSON format rather than plain text

## Related Resources

For deeper investigations, you can extend your analysis using:
- The full checkpoint context via `checkpoint explain`
- A comprehensive provenance investigation workflow

This tool is useful when you need to understand the developmental history behind any piece of code.

# Data Exchange Types Between Entire CLI and Agent Integrations

Based on the documentation, there are three primary data types exchanged:

## 1. HookInput
Passed via stdin to `get-session-id` and `read-session` hooks. Contains lifecycle events with:
- **Core fields**: `hook_type`, `session_id`, `session_ref`, `timestamp`
- **Optional fields**: `user_prompt`, `tool_name`, `tool_use_id`, `tool_input`, `raw_data`
- **Hook types**: session_start, session_end, user_prompt_submit, stop, pre_tool_use, post_tool_use

## 2. AgentSession
Exchanged between CLI and `write-session`/`read-session` endpoints. Tracks:
- Session metadata (`session_id`, `agent_name`, `repo_path`, `start_time`)
- File tracking: `modified_files`, `new_files`, `deleted_files`
- `native_data` field for "opaque session content in agent's native format"

## 3. Event
Normalized lifecycle representation returned by `parse-hook`. Contains:
- Numeric `type` (1-7 representing SessionStart through SubagentEnd)
- Session identifiers and timestamps
- Optional fields: `prompt`, `model`, `tool_use_id`, `subagent_id`, `metadata`

**Note**: The documentation provided doesn't include JSON structure details for metadata.json or checkpoint schemas—only the three core data model structures are documented.

# Checkpoint Storage in Git Refs

## Ref Namespace and Structure

Checkpoints stored using ref-based backend (`git-refs`) are organized at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, where the shard consists of "the last two characters of the ID" and the ID remains at the leaf position.

## What Each Ref Points To

Each ref points to "a commit whose tree root is that one checkpoint's contents." This means the commit contains the complete checkpoint data organized as a tree structure, rather than storing metadata and transcripts separately in a flat format.

## Checkpoint Identification

Under ref-based storage, checkpoints use "26-character, time-sortable ULID" identifiers (example: `01KVBJCWYA4YW6J5M9GP655HZN`). This differs from the branch-based backend, which uses 12-character hexadecimal IDs.

## Reading Checkpoints Externally

You can inspect checkpoint refs using standard Git commands without Entire installed:

```bash
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/
```

This lists all per-checkpoint refs. To view the complete checkpoint tree for a specific ref, use `git show <ref>` or examine its contents with standard Git inspection tools.

## Key Advantage

"Multiple agents can save checkpoints at once without competing to update one branch," since each checkpoint has its own independent ref rather than all sharing a single branch tip.

# entire-graph Overview

**How it works:**
entire-graph analyzes repositories locally by mapping "files, symbols, and relationships such as callers, callees, and type usage." It also leverages limited Git history to identify frequently co-changing files, without transmitting code externally.

**Capabilities:**
Yes, it can answer "what does this file affect." The tool traces relationships including callers, callees, type usage, and "potential impact" through commands like `impact`, `neighbors`, and `def`. This enables understanding code connections before making changes.

**Language support:**
It provides full semantic analysis for 36 languages (Python, JavaScript, Go, Rust, Java, etc.) with relationship tracing, plus basic file/symbol structure recognition for 149 additional filetypes.

**Output format:**
The documentation references JSON output—you can run `entire graph capabilities --json` to see supported features, though specific output schema details aren't provided in this content.

**Installation:**
It's installed as a repository-level tool that must be "installed and enabled for a repository" before agents can use it. The setup guides and CLI reference contain detailed installation instructions (linked but not excerpted here).

**Limitation:**
entire-graph may miss dynamically created connections through reflection, interfaces, or generated code, so results should be treated as a starting point rather than definitive analysis.

# entire-graph Command Reference Summary

**entire-graph** is a CLI plugin enabling codebase analysis for coding agents. Here's what it does:

## Core Capabilities

The tool provides semantic code search and impact analysis. As stated in the documentation, it "gives your coding agent a map of your codebase" to help locate relevant code and understand dependencies before making edits.

## Key Commands

**Search & Discovery:**
- `graph search` — Finds code regions matching plain-language queries, with results ranked by relevance
- `graph def` — Displays symbol declarations including fields, methods, and implementations
- `graph explain` — Enriches build/test failures with symbol definitions

**Relationship Analysis:**
- `graph impact` — Reveals callers, callees, type consumers, and affected files for any symbol
- `graph neighbors` — Shows direct relationships filtered by connection type and direction

**Change Tracking:**
- `graph commit` — Lists entity-level changes within a commit
- `graph diff` — Compares symbol changes between Git references
- `graph verify` — Executes tests and reports which ones changed state

**Data Export:**
- `graph snapshot` — Exports the complete graph as NDJSON
- `graph symbols` / `graph edges` — Export specific record types

## Notable Features

The `impact` command outputs a "blast radius" showing how many callers/callees and co-change files exist for a symbol. Search results include signal metadata explaining ranking factors like "path," "body," or "graph:callers."

content.content:
# Checkpoint Creation Process

## How Agent Work Becomes a Checkpoint

The documentation describes a two-stage process:

1. **Agent hooks** capture session context (prompts, transcript, tool activity, changed files, token usage)
2. **Git hooks** link that context to a commit by adding an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer

## What Triggers Checkpoint Creation

A checkpoint requires two things:
- Captured session context from agent work
- A Git commit

When you run `git commit` after agent work, Entire detects the activity and prompts: *"Link this commit to session context? [Y]es / [n]o / [a]lways"*

## commit_linking Modes

The documentation distinguishes three modes:
- **Prompt mode** (default): You decide for each commit whether to link
- **yes/no**: One-time decision for that specific commit
- **always**: Automatically link matching commits without prompting

Set this in `.entire/settings.json` or `.entire/settings.local.json`

## Metadata Contents

The documentation **does not list individual metadata.json fields**. It only mentions that Entire stores "checkpoint metadata" in your repository via Git ref or checkpoints branch.

## Technical Implementation

The document doesn't specify:
- Whether the trailer is added via post-commit, commit-msg, or amend hook
- Whether network/login is required
- Whether it works fully offline

The guide focuses on user-facing workflow rather than implementation details.

I found relevant information about the Databricks SDK for Python and the Statement Execution API. Here are the key results:

## Statement Execution API

The Databricks SQL Statement Execution API can be used to execute SQL statements on a SQL warehouse and fetch the result. Statement execution begins by issuing a statementexecution/executeStatement request with a valid SQL statement and warehouse ID, along with optional parameters such as the data catalog and output format.

## Using with Delta Tables and INSERT

The Statement Execution API can be used to execute INSERT statements against Delta tables. The `w.statement_execution.execute()` method from the Databricks SDK allows you to execute SQL statements like "CREATE TABLE" and can work with catalogs and schemas.

For example, you can insert data into a Delta table using an INSERT statement passed to the Statement Execution API. When you INSERT INTO a Delta table, schema enforcement and evolution is supported, and if a column's data type cannot be safely cast to a Delta table's data type, a runtime exception is thrown.

## Key Features

- If no other parameters are specified, the server will wait for up to 10s before returning a response. If the statement has completed within this timespan, the response will include the result data as a JSON array and metadata. Otherwise, the response will provide the statement ID that can be used to poll for results.

The search results include official Databricks documentation and SDK references that cover these capabilities.

# Entire Glossary: Key Concepts

Based on the documentation provided, here are the essential terms:

**Checkpoint**: "A save point for your work. Entire creates checkpoints around agent activity and links committed ones to Git commits."

**Session**: "A complete interaction with an AI coding agent from start to finish. Sessions include prompts, responses, code changes, checkpoints, token usage, metadata, and line attribution."

**Shadow Branch**: A temporary local Git branch storing checkpoints during active work, named like `entire/<sessionID>-<worktreeID>` and never pushed remotely.

**Checkpoint Ref**: The Git reference storing a single checkpoint under the ref-based backend at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`.

**Commit Linking**: The connection between a Git commit and its corresponding Entire checkpoint, preserving the session context that produced the code.

# Summary of `entire blame`

The `entire blame` command provides **git-blame-style line attribution enriched with Entire checkpoint metadata**. It shows which commit introduced each line and tags commits by type:

- **AI**: Attributed to an AI agent session
- **MX**: Mixed AI and human-attributed work
- **HU**: Made without AI checkpoint data

## Key Capabilities

You can filter output using `--line` (specific lines or ranges), display extended details with `--long`, or export as JSON via `--json`. The tool optionally links lines to their checkpoint metadata including agent info, model details, author, and session information.

## Usage Example

```bash
entire blame overview.mdx --line 12-20 --long
```

This displays lines 12–20 with full attribution context.

## Related Tools

The documentation suggests exploring the `why` command for deeper context on why specific code exists, and reviewing the "Investigate Why Code Exists" guide for tracing surprising lines back to checkpoint data.

# Summary of `entire import`

## What It Imports
The `entire import` command allows you to "Import pre-existing local agent transcripts for the current repository as read-only checkpoints." It specifically scans agent transcript stores from the past month for supported applications like Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot CLI, and others.

## Key Characteristics
Imported checkpoints have these properties:
- **Read-only** and searchable
- **Idempotent** — already-imported turns are automatically skipped
- **Not rewindable** or linked to Git commits
- **Explainable** for transparency

## Flags Available
- `--dry-run`: Preview what would be imported without creating checkpoints
- `--path DIRECTORY`: Specify a custom transcript location
- `--session ID`: Import only specific session identifiers (repeatable)

## Login Requirements
The documentation doesn't explicitly state login requirements, though the command operates on local transcript stores specific to your repository.

## Checkpoint References & Commits
Imported checkpoints are "not linked to a Git commit," so they don't create automatic commit references. This makes the feature useful for demo setups where you want historical context without live agent activity generating new sessions.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, indefinitely** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Timeout → killed. Set `persistent: true` for session-length watches (PR monitoring, log tails) — the monitor runs until you call TaskStop or the session ends. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms, max 3600000ms. Ignored when persistent is true.

persistent.description: Run for the lifetime of the session (no timeout). Use for session-length watches like PR monitoring or log tails. Stop with TaskStop.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.content:
# Checkpoint Overview

## What Is a Checkpoint?

A checkpoint serves as "an addressable record of the context behind an AI-assisted change." The system captures this data through Git hooks and agent integrations whenever work occurs, then saves it upon commit and links it to that commit via metadata.

## Captured Data

Checkpoints preserve:
- The associated Git commit
- Agent session information (one or multiple)
- Prompts and conversation transcripts
- Tool execution logs
- Modified files
- Token consumption metrics
- AI attribution data showing which lines were AI-generated

## Commit Linking

Entire integrates checkpoint identification into the commit process through an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer added to commit messages. The checkpoint metadata resides within the repository itself, stored either as a Git ref or on a checkpoints branch depending on your configured storage backend. This approach maintains a clean Git history without extraneous commits.

## Key Value Propositions

Checkpoints enable developers to review agent activities with full context, trace commits back to their originating prompts and sessions, understand the reasoning behind changes, and search historical agent work.

## Note on Condensed vs. Pending

The provided documentation excerpt does not address condensed versus pending checkpoint states or their specific schemas.

# Entire CLI: Technical Architecture & Roadmap

## Checkpoint Creation & Storage

**Creation Process:**
The CLI operates as "an invisible layer capturing everything in the background" during normal developer workflows. Checkpoints are created at two stages:
- **Pre-commit:** Temporary Checkpoint data stored outside the working branch as "rewind points during a session"
- **Post-commit:** Permanent Checkpoint linked to commits via a Git trailer

**Storage Architecture:**
The system uses "Git as a database" rather than proprietary systems. Checkpoint metadata (transcripts, prompts, attribution, summaries) are stored as Git objects. Teams can choose between:
- Same repository as code (default)
- Separate repository for privacy/management

## Git Integration Details

**Checkpoint ID Storage:**
"A Checkpoint ID is stored in a commit trailer rather than derived from the commit hash." This design allows the connection to "survive common history-rewriting operations such as rebase, amend, squash, and cherry-pick."

**Git Hooks:**
The document does not specify which Git hooks are used (post-commit, etc.).

## Metadata Captured

According to the spec, Checkpoints include:
- Code state
- Agent transcript
- Developer prompts
- Token usage
- "Line-level attribution showing what came from the agent and what was edited by the developer"

## Offline/Local Operation

The document states Checkpoint capture "happens locally, an individual developer can use Checkpoints without requiring the whole team to change its CI setup or workflow." No login requirement is mentioned.

## Roadmap

Four planned features:
1. **Team Visibility** – Context about agents involved, token usage, sessions
2. **Search** – Query reasoning behind changes and prompts
3. **Audit & Transparency** – Provenance tracking
4. **Intent Review** – Review based on prompts and session history before code inspection

## API, MCP & Programmatic Access

No mentions of MCP, APIs, or programmatic access are included in this document.

# entire-graph Installation and Setup

## Installation Command
Install using: `entire plugin install graph`

Verify with: `entire graph version`

## Enabling in Repository
Run from your repo root: `entire graph init-agents --repo .`

This creates/updates three files:
- `.entire/graph-agent.md` (agent operating guide)
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` (instruction files with managed blocks)

Then commit these files to share the setup with your team.

## Login and Network Requirements
The documentation provided does not specify whether login or network access is required for installation or operation.

The documentation does not detail where the index is stored or how long indexing takes. It mentions that "entire-graph maps your code" but doesn't explain the indexing mechanics or performance characteristics.

## Key Prerequisite
The setup requires "Git 2.36 or later" since entire-graph uses the "single-session object protocol that version added to check an object's type before reading its contents."

############ agent-help ############
Entire's CLI is the source of truth for its own usage. Do not guess flags or
subcommands — read them from this command. You are already inside the repo:
entire auto-detects it from the git origin remote, so never ask the user for the
repo name. Pass --repo only to target a DIFFERENT repo.

Current repo: not auto-detectable here (no origin remote / detached HEAD); pass --repo explicitly.

When to use entire — the commands that bear on the work:
  checkpoint  Inspect and search checkpoints
                read-only except: policy
  search      Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
                read-only
  session     Manage agent sessions tracked by Entire
                read-only except: adopt, attach, resume, stop
  status      Show Entire status
                read-only
  why         Show why a line exists
                read-only

Also available (entire agent-help <command> for any of these):
  read-only, safe to run:
    activity · blame · experts · labs · recap · tokens · version
  when the task needs them:
    api · dispatch · doctor · import · runner
  the user's — suggest, don't run:
    agent · auth · clean · configure · disable · enable · grant
    investigate · login · logout · org · plugin · project · repo
    review

Drill in for exact, currently-installed flags:  entire agent-help <command>  (e.g. entire agent-help checkpoint)
Add --json for structured output.

############ checkpoint --help ############
Operations on checkpoints — the persistent records of agent work tied to commits.

Commands:
  list     List checkpoints on the current branch
  explain  Explain a checkpoint, commit, or session
  tokens   Show token usage and optimization recommendations
  search   Search checkpoints (semantic + keyword)

Examples:
  entire checkpoint list
  entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>
  entire checkpoint tokens <id>
  entire checkpoint search "fix login"

Usage:
  entire checkpoint [command]

Aliases:
  checkpoint, cp, checkpoints

Experimental commands:
  policy      Inspect and update checkpoint policy

Additional Commands:
  explain     Explain a session, commit, or checkpoint
  list        List checkpoints on the current branch
  search      Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
  tokens      Show token usage and optimization recommendations for a checkpoint

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for checkpoint

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

Use "entire checkpoint [command] --help" for more information about a command.

############ checkpoint list --help ############
List checkpoints on the current branch.

By default shows condensed checkpoints from the checkpoints branch for the
current branch. Use --pending for the resume view instead: live checkpoints on
the session's shadow branch (not yet condensed), plus logs-only resume points
recovered from commits whose logs are already condensed.

Output modes:
  --json             Machine-readable JSON instead of the human view.
  --pending          Select the pending dataset: live shadow-branch
                     checkpoints plus logs-only resume points.
  --pending --json   Pending checkpoints as JSON (replaces the deprecated rewind --list).

Optionally filter condensed checkpoints by session ID with --session
(not applicable with --pending).

Usage:
  entire checkpoint list [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for list
      --json             Output as JSON instead of the human view
      --no-pager         Disable pager output
      --pending          List pending checkpoints — live shadow-branch state plus logs-only resume points
      --session string   Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

############ checkpoint explain --help ############
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo owner/name
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

Usage:
  entire checkpoint explain [checkpoint-id | commit-sha] [flags]

Flags:
  -c, --checkpoint string             Explain a specific checkpoint (ID or prefix)
      --commit string                 Explain a specific commit (SHA or ref, "commit-ish")
      --force                         Regenerate summary even if one already exists (requires --generate)
      --full                          Show full parsed transcript (all prompts/responses)
      --generate                      Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
  -h, --help                          help for explain
      --insecure-http-auth            Allow plain-HTTP auth for --repo (local dev only)
      --json                          Output metadata as JSON (no transcript bytes)
      --limit int                     Cap the list view at N checkpoints (default: 100). Only meaningful with --json.
      --no-pager                      Disable pager output
      --raw-transcript                Show raw transcript file (JSONL format)
      --repo string                   Explain a checkpoint owned by another repo (owner/name or gh/owner/name), read from that repo's Entire API
      --search-all                    Search all commits (no branch/depth limit, may be slow)
      --session string                Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)
      --session-index int             Session index within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based, defaults to latest) (default -1)
  -s, --short                         Show summary only (omit prompts and files)
      --summary-timeout-seconds int   Hard deadline in seconds for --generate summary generation; overrides summary_timeout_seconds setting. 0 = use setting; if setting is also unset or 0, no automatic deadline applies.
      --transcript                    Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes to stdout

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)
